question: Which kitchen layout suits my room?
answer: The right layout depends on room shape, size, and how you cook. STRAIGHT (single-wall) suits apartments and studios · GALLEY (two parallel runs) suits narrow rooms and gives the best cooking workflow · L-SHAPED (two adjoining walls) is the most versatile for family homes · U-SHAPED (three walls) maximises storage and workspace for serious cooks · ISLAND kitchens work when the room is at least 3.5m x 3.5m to allow 900mm+ walkway around the island · PENINSULA is the compromise when the room can't fit a full island. Send a rough sketch or measurement and we can recommend based on your specific room.

question: How much storage do I need in a kitchen?
answer: A useful rule: allow about 300mm of base cabinet width per person plus 300mm for every regularly-used appliance. So a family of four needs at least 1.2m of base cabinets plus 1.2m for oven/dishwasher/fridge appliances. Wall cabinets add roughly 60% more storage on top. Tall pantry units are more efficient than the equivalent base + wall cabinet combination. Corner cabinets need pull-out or carousel mechanisms to be usable.

question: Which worktop is best for my budget?
answer: Under £1,500 (economy): LAMINATE gives huge design choice and easy cleaning · under £2,500 (mid): SOLID WOOD (oak/walnut/maple) adds warmth but needs regular oiling · £2,000-£4,500 (premium): QUARTZ is scratch/stain/hygiene champion and no sealing · £3,000-£6,000 (luxury): PORCELAIN or SINTERED STONE is heat/UV/scratch proof and works indoor + outdoor · GRANITE and MARBLE are natural stone luxury options. Tell us your budget and we'll match the best material.

question: What cabinet door style suits a modern home?
answer: For contemporary/modern homes: SLAB (flat, unfussy) · HANDLELESS (J-pull or true handleless) · matt finishes · dark or neutral colours. Shaker works in modern homes too when kept slim-profile with painted finish. Avoid raised panel, beaded, and in-frame styles for pure modern — they read traditional. If your home mixes eras (contemporary furniture in a Victorian house), Slim Shaker is the safest bridge.

question: Should I choose an island or a peninsula?
answer: ISLAND wins when you have space (3.5m+ x 3.5m+ room · at least 900mm walkway on all four sides). Islands give the best social cooking + extra worksurface + open-plan flow · they can house sink, hob, seating, storage. PENINSULA wins when the room can't fit a full island — it gives you 3 sides of extra worksurface and often seating without needing the 4th walkway. Choose peninsula in kitchens smaller than about 3.5m in the narrow dimension.

question: How much space is needed around a kitchen island?
answer: Minimum 900mm walkway on every side of the island (1000mm+ preferred, especially on the cook side where oven doors need to open). If the island is used for seating on one side, allow 1000mm behind seated diners. Never squeeze walkways below 900mm — the kitchen will feel cramped and appliance doors will not open properly. Send the room dimensions and we'll design the largest island that fits comfortably.

question: Which appliances should I buy?
answer: The essential four for most families: OVEN (single or double) · HOB (induction is safest and fastest to clean; gas offers wok cooking; ceramic is budget) · EXTRACTOR (matched to hob width, external venting is quieter than recirculation) · DISHWASHER (integrated for clean lines, or freestanding for budget). Add as needed: MICROWAVE, WINE COOLER, BOILING WATER TAP, COFFEE MACHINE. Integrated appliances give cleaner lines but cost 20-40% more than freestanding equivalents.

question: What lighting works best in a kitchen?
answer: Layer three types of light. AMBIENT (general ceiling lighting — recessed downlights on a dimmer are the workhorse) · TASK (under-cabinet LED strips over worktops, over the hob, over the sink — cool white for tasks) · FEATURE (island pendants for social atmosphere, plinth LEDs for evening glow, in-cabinet lighting for glazed display units). All three on separate switches so you can adjust the mood. A kitchen with only ambient lighting feels flat; one with all three feels premium.

question: Which kitchen colours increase house value?
answer: Neutral colours age best and appeal to the widest buyer pool: WHITE (still the most requested), CASHMERE, STONE GREY, and NATURAL OAK are the safest. SAGE GREEN, NAVY BLUE, and GRAPHITE have grown from trend to established option and don't feel dated. Very dark colours (matt BLACK, deep GREEN, bold RED) look striking but polarise buyers — great for staying, riskier for reselling within 5 years. Two-tone kitchens (dark base + light wall units, or navy island + white cabinets) are the current premium look.

question: How do I plan a kitchen renovation?
answer: Six stages in order: (1) DECIDE SCOPE — new kitchen only, or extension/walls out? (2) SET BUDGET — allow 15-25% contingency; typical bespoke kitchen £15k-£40k+ (3) SITE VISIT + DESIGN — 2-4 weeks including revisions (4) MANUFACTURING — 4-10 weeks depending on supplier (5) INSTALL — typically 1-3 weeks (6) DECORATION + AFTERCARE — 1-2 weeks. Order appliances early — some have 12+ week lead times. Never remove the old kitchen until the new one is ready to install.

question: How much does a new kitchen cost?
answer: UK ranges (kitchen supply + fit, excluding appliances + electrical + plastering): FLAT-PACK ENTRY £3k-£8k · MID-RANGE FITTED £8k-£20k · BESPOKE £20k-£50k · HANDMADE LUXURY £50k-£150k+. Add appliances £2k-£15k depending on brand and features. Add £1.5k-£4k for electrical + plumbing + plastering + decoration. Islands typically add 20-30% to the kitchen cost. Get 3 quotes with matching specifications for a fair comparison.

question: What's the difference between MDF, plywood, and solid wood kitchen cabinets?
answer: MDF (medium-density fibreboard): stable, uniform, takes paint beautifully, cost-effective — the most common material for painted cabinets and doors. Not moisture-resistant unless it's MR-MDF. PLYWOOD: layered timber sheets, stronger and lighter than MDF, more moisture-tolerant, holds screws better — better for cabinet carcasses where strength matters. SOLID WOOD: real timber (oak, ash, walnut) — natural grain, warm, can be sanded and refinished, but expands/contracts with humidity. Most bespoke kitchens combine: MDF for painted doors + plywood for carcasses + solid wood for face frames.

question: Which kitchen style suits a Victorian home?
answer: Traditional Victorians (1837-1901) suit SHAKER (both traditional wide-frame and slim-profile · painted in heritage colours like sage, olive, navy, deep green), IN-FRAME (the most authentic period style), CLASSIC RAISED-PANEL, or FARMHOUSE with Belfast sink and freestanding elements. Add cornices, pilasters, and painted timber worktops for full period fidelity. Avoid pure MODERN or INDUSTRIAL — they fight the period detailing. Contemporary Shaker with quartz worktops is the most-chosen middle-ground for Victorian family homes.

question: How do I maximise storage in a small kitchen?
answer: Ten proven tactics: (1) TALL PANTRY UNITS instead of separate base + wall (2) DRAWER-STACK base cabinets — drawers hold more than cupboards (3) CORNER SOLUTIONS — Le Mans, magic corner, or diagonal cabinet (4) INTERNAL DRAWERS inside base cabinets (5) TALL HANDLELESS pull-out larder next to fridge (6) OVER-HOB shelf for spices (7) MAGNETIC KNIFE STRIP on splashback (8) TALL WALL CABINETS to ceiling — no dead space above (9) PLINTH DRAWERS for flat items like baking trays (10) UNDER-SINK cabinet with pull-out storage. Combined, these can double the effective storage of the same footprint.

question: What are the five main kitchen work zones?
answer: Every well-designed kitchen is built around five zones: (1) FOOD STORAGE — fridge/freezer/pantry, positioned near the entrance for easy grocery unloading (2) PREPARATION — main worktop, chopping, small appliance storage, ideally between sink and hob (3) COOKING — oven/hob/extractor/microwave, with heat-resistant worktop on both sides of the hob (4) CLEANING — sink/dishwasher/waste/recycling, near the preparation zone (5) STORAGE — base + wall + tall units + drawers + organisers. The 'work triangle' (sink-hob-fridge) still matters but modern designs use the five-zone model for larger and open-plan kitchens.

question: What's the difference between Shaker and In-Frame kitchen doors?
answer: SHAKER doors have a flat panel inside a five-piece frame (top rail, bottom rail, two stiles, centre panel). The door sits on the FRONT of the cabinet with a small overlay — the frame appears as part of the door itself. IN-FRAME doors sit INSIDE the cabinet frame (like a picture in a picture frame) — you see the cabinet's rails and stiles around every door. In-frame is more expensive (typically 20-40% more) because it requires precise carcass construction and hinges. In-frame is the more traditional look; Shaker suits both traditional and modern homes.

question: What is a handleless kitchen and what are the options?
answer: HANDLELESS means the doors and drawers open without visible handles. Three options: (1) TRUE HANDLELESS — a recessed grip channel is routed into the top edge of doors and drawer fronts; the cleanest look, most expensive (2) J-PULL — a J-shaped profile is integrated into the top edge; simpler and cheaper, gives an angled grip point (3) PUSH-TO-OPEN — no handle or channel at all, cabinets open with a light push; ultra-minimal but not always practical near sink zones where wet hands press it accidentally. Handleless is a strong choice for modern and contemporary interiors; less suited to traditional homes.

question: What is quartz worktop and how does it differ from granite?
answer: QUARTZ worktops are engineered — approximately 90-95% natural quartz stone crushed and bound with resin, then colour-controlled. GRANITE is 100% natural stone cut from a slab. Differences: quartz is UNIFORM in colour and pattern (predictable · every slab matches); granite is UNIQUE per slab (every kitchen slightly different). Quartz is NON-POROUS (no sealing ever); granite is POROUS (needs sealing periodically). Quartz is generally more scratch/stain resistant. Granite is more heat resistant (you can put a hot pan down — though we don't recommend it on either). Price similar for mid-tier options; both are premium.

question: Should I choose induction, gas or ceramic hob?
answer: INDUCTION is now the recommended default for most homes: fastest to boil, safest (surface stays cool except where the pan is), easiest to clean, most energy-efficient · requires induction-compatible pans (most modern stainless and cast iron work). GAS suits serious cooks who want wok cooking or visible flame control and don't mind the harder cleaning · needs gas supply. CERAMIC is the budget electric option · slower and less efficient than induction · being phased out by most premium brands. Induction wins on 8/10 criteria for family homes; gas wins for enthusiast cooks; ceramic only wins on price.

question: What is a butler's pantry and do I need one?
answer: A butler's pantry is a small utility kitchen space adjacent to the main kitchen — traditionally used for prep, appliance storage, and dish washing so the main kitchen stays presentable when entertaining. Modern butler's pantries typically include a sink + dishwasher + coffee station + extra storage + microwave hidden away. You need one if: you entertain often, want your main kitchen to stay pristine, have space for a 2m x 2m+ separate room. You don't need one if: your main kitchen has enough storage, you live alone or with just a partner, budget is tight (a butler's pantry adds £8k-£20k).

question: What kitchen sink type should I choose?
answer: UNDERMOUNT (fitted below the worktop, no visible sink rim) — cleanest lines, easy to wipe crumbs straight in, requires worktop that supports undermount (quartz/granite/porcelain, not laminate) · INSET (drops into a cutout, has a visible rim) — works with any worktop, cheaper, slight lip to clean around · BELFAST or FARMHOUSE (front-facing apron) — heritage look, deep bowl, requires specific cabinet design · INTEGRATED (moulded into a solid-surface worktop) — seamless, premium price. Single-bowl is better for large pans; 1.5 or 2 bowls for washing + drying simultaneously.

question: What is the difference between rigid, flat-pack, and bespoke kitchens?
answer: FLAT-PACK: cabinets arrive as flat sheets requiring assembly on-site. Cheapest, slower install, more risk of alignment issues. Suits budget projects. RIGID: cabinets arrive factory-assembled (already glued and screwed together). Stronger construction, faster install, better alignment. Now the most common mid-market option. BESPOKE: cabinets are made to exact measurements for your specific room — non-standard widths, custom heights, unique storage solutions. Premium price and 6-10 week lead time but zero wasted space and full design flexibility.

question: How long does it take to fit a new kitchen?
answer: Typical install duration: RIP-OUT + PREP 2-3 days · CARCASS INSTALL 2-4 days · WORKTOP TEMPLATE + FIT 3-7 days (worktop fitters visit after cabinets are in to template accurately, then return with the cut worktop) · APPLIANCE + PLUMBING + ELECTRICAL 2-3 days · SNAG + FINISH 1-2 days. Total: 2-3 weeks for most fitted kitchens · up to 4-5 weeks for bespoke handmade kitchens with extensive tiling and decoration. Add 2-3 more weeks if walls need moving or floors laid.

question: What kitchen ventilation regulations do I need to follow?
answer: UK Building Regulations (Approved Document F) require kitchen mechanical ventilation. Options: EXTRACTOR HOOD over the hob venting EXTERNALLY (recommended · minimum 60 l/s extract rate) · WALL-MOUNTED EXTRACT FAN (if hood is recirculating only · minimum 30 l/s in a kitchen without a cooker hood) · PASSIVE STACK VENTILATION (older/less common approach). Recirculating hoods without external duct do NOT satisfy the requirement on their own — you need a separate extract fan too. If installed as part of a full kitchen renovation, ventilation is checked at building control sign-off.

question: What are corner cabinet solutions?
answer: Corner cabinets are the most difficult storage space in any kitchen. Five common solutions: (1) LE MANS (two swing-out kidney-shaped shelves that pull the contents into view) — premium, best for deep corners (2) MAGIC CORNER (a full-extension pull-out with a secondary tray that swings out with the door) — excellent capacity (3) CAROUSEL (rotating shelves on a central pole) — cheapest, common in flat-pack (4) BLIND CORNER PULL-OUT (a full-extension frame that pulls the entire corner content out) — deep-storage friendly (5) DIAGONAL CORNER CABINET (a diamond-shaped cabinet with a single door) — no fancy mechanism, straightforward but wastes some space. Never leave a corner as an unfitted dead space.

question: What worktop overhang can I have on a kitchen island?
answer: For a seating overhang (bar-stool side), 300mm is the practical minimum for comfortable knee room; 400mm is preferred; 500mm needs support brackets or corbels underneath (or thick worktop of 30mm+). Quartz and porcelain can span up to 300mm unsupported when 20mm thick; more than that needs a hidden steel bracket or a thicker worktop. Never rely on cabinet-only support for overhangs over 300mm — the worktop will crack over time under weight.

question: What is a broken-plan kitchen?
answer: BROKEN-PLAN means the kitchen is partially — not fully — separated from adjoining living/dining spaces. Uses partial dividers: glass partitions, timber slat screens, half-walls (dwarf walls), open shelving units, or a peninsula acting as the boundary. Popular because it keeps the light and connection of open-plan living, but creates defined zones and blocks cooking mess/smells more effectively than fully open-plan. Best for family homes where cooking smells and noise need containing without losing the sociable feel.

question: What appliances go in a Scandinavian-style kitchen?
answer: SCANDINAVIAN style favours integrated appliances hidden behind matching cabinet fronts — no visible branding, no stainless steel. Typical fit-out: INTEGRATED FRIDGE-FREEZER (full-height, tall unit) · INTEGRATED DISHWASHER · INDUCTION HOB (flush-fitted, no protruding controls) · CEILING-MOUNTED or DOWNDRAFT EXTRACTOR (avoids visible hood) · OVEN + COMBI MICROWAVE stacked in a tall unit (not visible from the main sitting angle) · BOILING WATER TAP replacing a kettle to keep worktops clear. The goal is a kitchen that reads as furniture, not as a room of appliances.

question: What is porcelain worktop and why is it becoming popular?
answer: PORCELAIN worktops are ultra-compact ceramic slabs fired at very high temperatures. Advantages: HEAT RESISTANT (you can put a hot pan directly on it), UV RESISTANT (doesn't fade in sunlight — the only worktop suitable for outdoor kitchens), WATERPROOF, SCRATCH RESISTANT, STAIN RESISTANT, and available in stunning marble/concrete/stone-look finishes at 6mm or 12mm slim profiles. Growing in premium kitchens because it combines the best properties of quartz + granite + solid surface. Slightly harder to work with (specialist installers only) and premium price (£350-£600 per m² typical), but the material of choice for luxury contemporary kitchens.

question: Which kitchen door style is the most timeless?
answer: SHAKER is the most timeless — it has been popular for 200+ years, works in Victorian townhouses, Georgian country homes, modern new-builds, and contemporary flats. Slim SHAKER (narrow 45-55mm frame) shifts it to the modern end; wider SHAKER (70-90mm frame) reads more traditional. Painted Shaker in a neutral colour (white, cashmere, sage, navy) is the safest choice if you may sell the house within 10 years. Second most timeless: SLAB (flat door) in a natural timber or matt colour — pure modern that doesn't date if kept neutral.

question: How do I measure my kitchen correctly?
answer: Measure length + width along each wall from corner to corner. Take diagonal measurements to check the room is square (if diagonals differ, walls aren't parallel). Record ceiling height in multiple places (older homes are rarely flat). Mark window heights, sill heights, door widths. Note radiators, boilers, chimney breasts, beams, columns, sockets, switches, water supplies, waste pipes. Photograph everything. If in doubt, wait for the professional survey — the manufacturer's measure is what quotes are based on, not yours.

question: Why is one kitchen quote 5000 pounds cheaper than another?
answer: Rarely a fair comparison. The difference usually comes from: cabinet material (chipboard vs plywood carcass) · hinge quality (basic vs Blum/Hettich soft-close) · door construction (5-piece vs one-piece) · worktop material and thickness · appliances included/excluded · installation included/excluded · plumbing and electrical works included/excluded · warranty length · fitting time. Ask each supplier to break their quote down line-by-line into the same categories, then compare like-for-like. The cheapest quote often becomes the most expensive once the missing items are added.

question: Should I choose a shaker or slab door?
answer: SHAKER (framed with recessed centre panel) suits almost every home — traditional through to modern, painted or natural timber, 200+ years of proven appeal. SLAB (flat, no frame) is pure modern/minimalist, best for contemporary interiors, apartments, handleless designs. If your home is traditional/period or you may sell within 10 years, choose Shaker. If your home is contemporary and you want the cleanest lines, choose slab. If unsure, SLIM SHAKER (45-55mm frame) bridges both worlds.

question: Which worktop resists heat best?
answer: PORCELAIN and SINTERED STONE resist heat best — you can put a hot pan directly on the surface (though the manufacturer will still recommend a trivet). GRANITE is also heat resistant (natural stone). QUARTZ is more heat sensitive than granite because the resin binder can discolour above about 150C — always use a trivet. LAMINATE and SOLID SURFACE are the least heat resistant — never place hot pans directly on them. If you regularly cook and place pans down without thinking, porcelain or sintered stone is the safer choice.

question: Are handleless kitchens practical for families?
answer: YES for most families — but consider the type. TRUE HANDLELESS with recessed grip channel is easy to grip and clean but more expensive. J-PULL gives an integrated angle grip at lower cost and works well. PUSH-TO-OPEN is the most minimal but can trigger accidentally with wet hands near sinks — avoid at sink zones. Family homes typically choose J-Pull for everyday cabinets + true handleless for feature areas. All are safer for young children than protruding handles (no head-height projections), and easier to wipe clean than handles that trap grime.

question: Can my staircase manufacturer also build my kitchen?
answer: Yes, in many cases. A professional staircase manufacturer already has 80-90 percent of the woodworking, joinery, CNC, finishing, and installation skills needed for kitchens. What they usually need to add is kitchen-specific knowledge: cabinet standards (base/wall/tall sizes) · appliance integration (ovens, dishwashers, fridges) · kitchen hardware (Blum/Hettich hinges + drawers) · plumbing coordination · electrical coordination · worktop templating and fitting · kitchen workflow ergonomics. If they have (or can add) those, they can produce a kitchen that equals or exceeds many standard suppliers — with the huge advantage that your staircase and kitchen can share timber, finish, and design language. See the trade-capability-crossover article for the full assessment.

question: Should my kitchen match my staircase?
answer: YES if both are visible from the same area (open-plan, kitchen with hallway view, or double-height space). They become the two largest design features of the home and should feel like one coordinated project. Match at least ONE of: timber species (oak with oak) · paint colour palette · metal finish (matt black · brushed brass · satin nickel) · flooring · overall style (modern · Shaker · traditional). Do not copy every detail — matching one or two elements is enough to create visual harmony without feeling repetitive. If the staircase is in a separate hallway, matching is less critical but still helpful for whole-home coherence.

question: How much of my renovation budget should go to the kitchen?
answer: Depends on renovation type: COSMETIC REFRESH 30-50 percent · FULL RENOVATION 25-40 percent · LUXURY RENOVATION 20-35 percent · NEW SELF-BUILD 15-30 percent. For a 100k renovation, expect 25-40k on the kitchen and 8-15k on the staircase. For a 300k luxury project, 60-90k kitchen and 30-60k staircase. Do not overspend on the kitchen at the expense of everything else — a balanced investment where kitchen/staircase/flooring/doors/lighting share the same quality tier produces a cohesive result. See kitchen-vs-staircase-budget-allocation.md for the full breakdown.

question: Where should I buy my kitchen?
answer: Depends on what matters most. LOWEST PRICE goes to DIY retailer. GOOD VALUE goes to kitchen retailer. PROFESSIONAL DESIGN goes to kitchen showroom. LUXURY FINISH goes to bespoke kitchen manufacturer. UNIQUE HANDMADE goes to local joinery company. MATCHING STAIRCASE + KITCHEN goes to bespoke staircase/joinery company that builds both. FULL HOME RENOVATION goes to interior design company. Never focus only on price — compare cabinet quality, door construction, drawer systems, hinges, warranty, installation experience, and ability to supply replacement parts. See kitchen-where-to-buy.md for the full comparison.

question: Do I need planning permission for a new kitchen?
answer: NO for replacing a kitchen within its existing footprint (no walls moved, no external changes) — this is permitted development. YES if you are removing internal walls (needs Building Control approval + structural engineer sign-off for load-bearing walls), building an extension, or making external changes (new windows, doors, ventilation openings). Building Regulations always apply to electrical works (Part P) and gas works. If in doubt, contact your local Building Control before starting. Never begin structural work without proper sign-off — retroactive certification is expensive.

question: What is the difference between MDF and plywood for kitchen carcasses?
answer: MDF (Medium Density Fibreboard) is denser and smoother with no grain — excellent for painted doors and decorative panels. PLYWOOD is cross-laminated timber veneers — stronger, lighter, better screw-holding, more moisture-tolerant. Premium bespoke kitchens use PLYWOOD carcasses (typically birch ply) + MDF painted doors + solid timber face frames. Mid-market factory kitchens use MFC (Melamine Faced Chipboard) for carcasses (cheaper, stable, easy to clean) + MDF or timber doors. MDF as a carcass material is possible but heavier and more expensive than MFC — not the first choice unless the whole cabinet is being painted or the customer wants premium construction. See kitchen-mdf-suitability.md for the full comparison.

question: How long does it take to have a bespoke kitchen made?
answer: Typical bespoke timeline: DESIGN + REVISIONS 2-4 weeks · DEPOSIT + ORDERING 1 week · MANUFACTURING 6-10 weeks (some 12+) · TEMPLATE + WORKTOP 2-3 weeks after cabinets install · INSTALLATION 2-4 weeks. Total 12-22 weeks from first design meeting to fully finished kitchen. Add lead time for appliances (some premium brands 12+ weeks) — order appliances in parallel with cabinets so they do not delay install. Rush jobs are possible but usually mean rush charges + compromised quality. Never begin the rip-out until manufacturing is complete and delivery dates are confirmed.

question: Which upgrades add the most value to a kitchen?
answer: For RESALE value: neutral doors (white, cashmere, sage, navy) · quartz worktops · integrated appliances · island (if room allows) · pantry storage · under-cabinet lighting. For LIVING value (your own enjoyment): whatever suits your lifestyle — a keen cook values a good hob + extractor + prep space more than resale-friendly neutrality. AVOID over-personalising (bright red cabinets, ultra-trendy colours) if you may sell within 5 years. AVOID under-investing in the invisible parts — hinges, drawer runners, cabinet construction — because they wear out first and are what makes a kitchen feel high-quality every day.

question: Should the flooring go under kitchen cabinets or stop at the plinth?
answer: USUALLY STOP AT THE PLINTH for fitted cabinets. Reasons: (1) cabinets sit on adjustable legs — the plinth conceals the leg and rests on the finished floor · (2) saves flooring cost (10-25 percent of floor area is under cabinets) · (3) makes future cabinet changes easier without damaging floor · (4) prevents floor expansion issues under heavy cabinets. EXCEPTIONS — run flooring under cabinets when: (1) the flooring is thin (LVT, laminate) and needs to lie level under a full room · (2) you may replace cabinets with a totally different layout · (3) you want the option to move cabinets easily later. For freestanding pieces (dressers, tables), always continue flooring underneath.

question: Is quartz or granite better for a family kitchen?
answer: QUARTZ wins for busy family kitchens. Non-porous (no sealing ever · resists stains from wine, curry, coffee, juice). Consistent colour and pattern (predictable · matches). Scratch-resistant. Hygienic (bacteria cannot penetrate). Only weakness: less heat-tolerant than granite (use a trivet for pans above 150C). GRANITE (natural stone) is more heat-resistant and each slab is unique · but porous (needs periodic sealing) and can stain if a spill sits. For families with children, spills, and busy weekday cooking, quartz is the safer, lower-maintenance choice. For a household with a keen chef who wants the character of natural stone and does not mind sealing, granite is beautiful.

question: How many electrical sockets do I need in a kitchen?
answer: Rule of thumb: TWO double sockets minimum per metre of worktop above the countertop, PLUS dedicated circuits for each fixed appliance (oven · hob · dishwasher · fridge · washing machine · extractor · lighting circuits at least 2). ISLANDS need 2-4 sockets (pop-up preferred for clean lines). Add: 2 USB-A/USB-C in the coffee/breakfast zone · 1 socket inside a tall pantry for a charging drawer · 1 socket for future appliance (leave a spare circuit at the consumer unit). NEVER go under-specced — retrofitting sockets after tiling is expensive and messy. UK regs: sockets minimum 150mm from sink zones; all kitchen sockets on RCD-protected circuit.

question: What lighting temperature should I use in a kitchen?
answer: Use MIXED temperatures on separate circuits: TASK LIGHTING (under-cabinet, over hob, over sink) is COOL WHITE 4000K-5000K for accurate colour when cooking and reading recipes. AMBIENT CEILING LIGHTING (downlights) is NEUTRAL WHITE 3000K-3500K for everyday use. FEATURE LIGHTING (pendants over island, plinth LEDs, in-cabinet glow) is WARM WHITE 2700K-3000K for atmosphere. All on dimmers where possible. Colour temperature affects mood — warm feels cozy, cool feels crisp and clean. Avoid single-temperature kitchens; the layering is what makes premium kitchens feel premium.

question: What questions should I ask before signing a kitchen contract?
answer: Ask: (1) What material are the carcasses? What thickness are the backs? (2) Which hinge and drawer brand? Soft-close throughout? (3) Are all shown appliances included or optional extras? (4) Is worktop templating included? Which worktop material and thickness? (5) Is installation included? By employed installers or subcontractors? (6) What warranty covers the cabinets, doors, hinges, drawers, worktops, appliances (separately)? (7) When will manufacturing start? When is delivery? When is install complete? (8) What is the payment schedule — deposit, interim, final? (9) What happens if a door is damaged in years 3, 5, 10? Can replacement doors be colour-matched? (10) What is the process for snag-list resolution? Get all answers in writing before paying the deposit.

question: Can I add more kitchen cabinets in a few years?
answer: YES if you plan for it. Choose a manufacturer that: (1) archives your specific timber species batch and paint colour code · (2) stocks or can re-order matching doors, drawers, hinges · (3) can extend the existing run without visible joins · (4) documents your exact spec (cabinet sizes, finishes, mouldings). Ask BEFORE ordering: Will matching cabinets be available in 5 years? In 10 years? Bespoke joinery workshops are usually best at this because they made your kitchen originally and can reproduce it. Flat-pack retailers frequently discontinue lines within 3-5 years — matching later becomes near-impossible. If future expansion is likely, factor this into your supplier choice from day one.

question: How do I make a small kitchen feel bigger?
answer: Ten proven tactics: (1) LIGHT COLOURS (white, cashmere, pale grey doors reflect light) · (2) HANDLELESS DOORS (visually cleaner, less busy) · (3) HIGH GLOSS or REFLECTIVE finishes (multiply light) · (4) TALL WALL CABINETS to ceiling (no dead space above · draws the eye up) · (5) UNDERCABINET + PLINTH LIGHTING (removes visual weight from base cabinets) · (6) LARGE-FORMAT FLOOR TILES (fewer grout lines equal larger perception) · (7) OPEN SHELVING (breaks up solid cabinet mass) · (8) MIRRORED or GLASS SPLASHBACK (reflects light + view) · (9) INTEGRATED APPLIANCES (visual continuity) · (10) SIMPLIFY the palette (max 2-3 colours + one accent). Also: keep worktops clutter-free · use pull-out storage instead of stacked cupboards · consider drawer stacks over cupboards.

question: What are the most common kitchen design mistakes?
answer: Top mistakes to avoid: (1) TOO FEW SOCKETS — plan double what you think · (2) INSUFFICIENT WORKTOP each side of the hob (need at least 300mm each side · 600mm preferred) · (3) FRIDGE DOOR OPENING INTO A WALKWAY · (4) ISLAND TOO CLOSE to perimeter (need 900mm+ walkway · 1000mm cook side) · (5) BINS FAR from the sink · (6) NO PANTRY when you could fit one · (7) WALL CABINETS not reaching the ceiling (dust trap + wasted storage) · (8) TRENDY COLOURS that date within 5 years · (9) UNDER-SPECC'D HINGES + DRAWERS (they wear out first) · (10) SKIMPING ON LIGHTING (one downlight circuit only). Fix these at design stage · they are expensive or impossible to fix later.

question: Should I choose an integrated or freestanding fridge?
answer: INTEGRATED (built-in, hidden behind a matching cabinet door): cleaner sight lines, cohesive look, standard 60cm width, matches handleless kitchens. Costs 20-40 percent more than freestanding · usually smaller capacity · replacement models must match the housing dimensions. FREESTANDING (visible on its own · often American-style side-by-side or French door): 20-40 percent cheaper for same capacity · larger internal volume · easier to replace with any brand · but visible as a statement or eyesore depending on interior style. Choose INTEGRATED for minimalist, high-end, small-to-medium kitchens where visual cleanliness matters. Choose FREESTANDING for large families needing maximum capacity, or industrial/professional-style kitchens where the appliance is celebrated as a feature.

question: When during a renovation should the kitchen be installed?
answer: Standard sequence: (1) STRUCTURAL work (walls · steels · openings) · (2) FIRST-FIX PLUMBING + ELECTRICS (pipes and cables in place · not connected yet) · (3) PLASTERING · (4) DECORATION FIRST COAT · (5) FLOORING (some prefer after cabinets — see kitchen-faq-044) · (6) KITCHEN CABINETS · (7) WORKTOP TEMPLATE + FIT (worktop supplier visits after cabinets are level) · (8) TILING / SPLASHBACK · (9) SECOND-FIX PLUMBING + ELECTRICS (connect appliances, sockets, switches, lights) · (10) FINAL DECORATION + TOUCH-UPS · (11) SNAG-LIST inspection · (12) HANDOVER. Total: 4-8 weeks depending on scope. Never install the kitchen before plastering is fully dry (moisture damages cabinets).

question: What worktop overhang is safe on a kitchen island for seating?
answer: UP TO 300mm: SAFE unsupported for a standard 20mm quartz/granite/porcelain worktop resting on a full cabinet run. 300-450mm: needs SUPPORT — either thicker worktop (30mm+) OR hidden steel brackets bolted to the cabinet frame OR decorative corbels underneath. 450mm+: MUST have visible or concealed structural support — never rely on cabinet-only support at this range · the worktop will crack over time under weight. For comfortable knee room while seated: 300mm is minimum · 400mm is preferred · 500mm is luxury. Timber worktops can support less overhang than stone before sagging. Never install seating overhangs without checking the manufacturer specific unsupported-span spec for the chosen worktop material.

question: Which kitchen appliance brands are most reliable?
answer: Reliability rankings shift year-to-year but consistent long-term leaders across UK/EU markets: MIELE (premium · 20+ year lifespan common · high initial cost but lowest long-term). BOSCH + NEFF (mid-premium · reliable · widely serviceable · good spare parts). SIEMENS (premium engineering shared with Bosch). AEG (mid-market · good design). SMEG (mid-premium · style-focused · slightly lower reliability scores). AVOID very cheap unbranded imports · service networks vanish. When choosing, prioritise: (1) spare-parts availability in 10 years, (2) local service engineer network, (3) warranty length + terms. Extended warranties beyond the standard 2 years are usually not cost-effective — buying a reliable brand upfront costs less than repair contracts.
